stages.title: Melody construction
stages.hook: Why can you hum some tunes after one hearing, while others slip away at once? What do the memorable ones have in common?
explain: A strong melody is built from small ideas. A motif is a short musical idea, a few notes with a recognisable rhythm. Composers repeat it, change it, or move it higher or lower (a sequence) to grow a whole tune.

Melodies move by steps (to the next note in the scale) or by leaps (skipping notes). Mostly stepwise tunes are smooth and singable; leaps add drama. The shape of a tune rising and falling is its contour, and a high point called the climax often comes near the end of a phrase.

Melodies are organised into phrases, like sentences. Two phrases often pair as a question and answer: the first ends on an unfinished note and the second ends on the tonic, the home note of the scale, which feels like arriving. Melody-making is found in every culture, from folk songs to ragas.

example.q: A motif is C C G G (as in the start of a famous nursery tune). Move it up a step to make a sequence. What notes?
steps: Original: C C G G.
Moving each note up one scale step gives D D A A.
The shape is the same at a new height.

analogies.home: A sentence has a beginning and an end. A phrase leaves you waiting or satisfied.
analogies.sport: A play in football builds up, then scores: a melody builds to a climax.
analogies.nature: A river bends gently, then drops in a waterfall: steps and leaps.
analogies.music: A motif is like a catchy riff that returns again and again.

terms: A short musical idea used to build a melody.
The up-and-down shape of a melody.
A musical sentence, often ending in a pause.
The home note of the scale.

misc.wrong: Good melodies use lots of different notes.
misc.right: Many great melodies use few notes and repeat a motif so people remember it.

trip.prompt: Find the section about contour. Match one of the contour shapes to a tune you know.

questions.q: What is a motif?
questions.why: A motif is a short, recognisable fragment from which melodies grow.

questions.q: What is a melody that moves note by note along the scale called?
questions.why: Stepwise motion moves to neighbouring notes.

questions.q: What does the tonic do at the end of a phrase?
o: Makes the tune suddenly much faster
Moves the music into a brand new key
Gives a feeling of arriving home
questions.why: The tonic is the home note and sounds settled.

questions.q: Listen. Which describes this tune?
questions.why: The notes 60 62 64 65 67 climb by step.

questions.q: Now listen to this tune. Which describes it?
questions.why: 60 to 72 to 67 to 79 jumps widely.

questions.q: A composer repeats a motif starting on a higher note. What is this called?
questions.why: Repeating a pattern at a different pitch is a sequence.

questions.q: Match the term to its meaning.
questions.why: These are building blocks of melody.

questions.q: Put these in the order a composer might build a tune.
questions.why: Small idea, development, phrase, then settle.

questions.q: Why do many memorable tunes repeat a short motif?
questions.model: Repetition makes the idea familiar and easy to remember, and short simple ideas are easy to sing.
questions.why: Repetition builds recognition.

questions.q: A phrase ends on the note above the tonic and sounds unfinished. What would make it sound complete?
o: Adding even more big leaps to it
Changing the beat of the music
Ending the next phrase on the tonic
questions.why: Answering with a tonic ending resolves the tension.

panel.q: A melody uses only leaps. What might a singer find?
o: It becomes very easy to sing
It turns into a smooth chord
It can be hard to sing and sound jagged
It has no rhythm left at all
panel.why: Wide jumps are harder to sing than steps.

panel.q: Explain how question-and-answer phrases create a satisfying shape.
panel.model: The first phrase ends open, which creates tension. The second answers by ending on the tonic, resolving it and sounding complete.
panel.why: Phrases work in pairs.

panel.q: A tune that goes up for a long time and then drops has its climax where?
o: At the lowest point of the tune
At the very start of the tune only
There is no climax in a tune like that
panel.why: The climax is the high point of the contour.

teach.model: A melody is built from a short motif, a small musical idea. You can repeat it, move it higher or lower, and join phrases together like sentences. A tune often ends on the tonic, the home note, so it feels finished.

points.ask: How do the parts fit together?

stages.title: Chord progressions
stages.hook: Thousands of songs share almost the same four chords. Why do they not all sound the same?
explain: A chord progression is a series of chords that supports a melody. Chords are numbered by their position in the scale using Roman numerals. In C major: I = C, ii = Dm, iii = Em, IV = F, V = G, vi = Am. Capitals are major, lower case are minor.

The most common progression in many styles is I – IV – V (C F G). Another famous pattern is I – V – vi – IV (C G Am F), used in pop and rock worldwide. Chords make tension and release: V often wants to go back to I, called a cadence, which works like a full stop.

The same progression can sound different with a different melody, rhythm, tempo or instruments, which is why many songs can share chords. The blues in particular uses a 12-bar pattern of I, IV and V chords.

example.q: In C major, what chords are I, IV, V?
steps: C major scale: C D E F G A B.
I is built on the 1st note, C; IV on the 4th, F; V on the 5th, G.
All three are major chords.

analogies.home: Story: beginning (home), adventure (away), return (home). Chords go on the same journey.
analogies.city: A route leaving the station, going round the city, back to the station.
analogies.sport: Offence builds and the goal ends the play: V to I.
analogies.music: V to I is like the full stop at the end of a sentence.

stages.mnemonic: One, four, five: the three-chord dive.
terms: A series of chords in order.
A symbol such as I or vi showing the chord position in the scale.
A chord ending that closes a phrase.
The V chord, which pulls strongly back to I.

misc.wrong: Songs with the same chords are copies.
misc.right: Melody, rhythm, lyrics and sound make each song unique, even if the chords match.

trip.prompt: Find the I–V–vi–IV example and name the chords in C major.

questions.q: In C major, which chord is IV?
questions.why: IV is built on the 4th note, F.

questions.q: In C major, which chord is V?
questions.why: V is built on the 5th note, G.

questions.q: In C major, which chord is vi?
questions.why: vi is built on the 6th note, A, and is minor.

questions.q: What do lower-case Roman numerals show?
questions.why: ii, iii and vi are minor in a major key.

questions.q: Listen. These chords are C then G. Which feels more unfinished?
questions.why: G is the dominant and leans back toward C, the home chord.

questions.q: What is a cadence?
o: A chord ending that closes a phrase
questions.why: Cadences work like punctuation.

questions.q: Match the Roman numeral to the chord in C major.
questions.why: Count scale degrees and note major or minor.

questions.q: Put the chords of I – V – vi – IV in C major in order.
questions.why: I is C, V is G, vi is Am, IV is F.

questions.q: Why can two different songs use the same progression and still sound different?
questions.model: The melody, rhythm, tempo, instruments and lyrics all differ, so the same chords can give very different songs.
questions.why: Chords are only one ingredient.

questions.q: A song in G major uses I – IV – V. What are the chords?
questions.why: G major scale: G A B C D E F♯. I = G, IV = C, V = D.

panel.q: Why does a V chord followed by I sound final?
o: V is just a louder chord than I
V creates tension that I releases
I is a lower note and nothing more
They are really the same chord
panel.why: The dominant leans toward the tonic.

panel.q: How does the 12-bar blues use only three chords and still feel complete?
panel.model: It cycles I, IV and V in a fixed 12-bar pattern. It leaves home, builds tension on the dominant and returns to I, so the cycle feels complete.
panel.why: Tension and return make the form.

panel.q: In the key of F major, the IV chord is
panel.why: F major scale: F G A B♭ C D E. The 4th note is B♭.

teach.model: A chord progression is a series of chords. We number chords by their place in the scale, so in C major I is C, IV is F and V is G. V pulls back to I, like a sentence ending. Many songs share the same chords but sound different.

points.ask: Why does V go to I?
Why don't songs sound the same?

stages.title: Rhythm and syncopation
stages.hook: Why does a rhythm that lands on the "off" beats make you want to move more than one that lands exactly on the beat?
explain: In simple metre, beats are counted 1 2 3 4 and the spaces between are "and": 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and. The "ands" are the offbeats. Syncopation is a rhythm that stresses weak or off positions, like the offbeats, or that holds a note across a strong beat. It creates surprise and a sense of push.

Syncopation is central to many styles. Reggae places its guitar or keyboard chop on the offbeats. Jazz, funk, hip hop and Afro-Cuban music use it heavily. Clave in Cuban music is a repeating five-stroke pattern that organises everything else. West African drumming layers rhythms that cross each other (polyrhythm).
A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound, often across a bar line, which is a simple way to write syncopation. The beat itself never changes; the accents move against it.

example.q: Count a bar of 4/4 with an eighth rest on beat 1 and eighth notes on the "and" of each beat. Where are the notes?
steps: Count: 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and.
Notes fall on every "and".
So they land on the offbeats.

analogies.home: Skipping stairs: you step between the numbers instead of on them.
analogies.sport: A basketball player dribbles to a beat but passes off it for surprise.
analogies.city: Walking in time while a street musician plays off the steps.
analogies.music: A drummer plays the hi-hat steady and the snare off the expected spot.

terms: The positions between the main beats, the "ands".
Stressing weak or off positions so the rhythm pushes against the beat.
A curve joining two notes of the same pitch into one.
Two or more different rhythms played together.

misc.wrong: Syncopation means the beat speeds up and slows down.
misc.right: The beat stays steady. The accents move away from the expected strong beats.

trip.prompt: Find a notated example. Mark where the unexpected accents land.

questions.q: What is syncopation?
o: Playing with no rhythm at all
Playing only on the first beat
questions.why: Syncopation shifts accents to unexpected places.

questions.q: In "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and", which are the offbeats?
questions.why: Offbeats fall between the numbered beats.

questions.q: A bar of 4/4 is counted 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and. A drummer plays only on the "ands". Where do the notes fall?
questions.why: The "ands" are the offbeats.

questions.q: Which style places chops on the offbeats as a trademark?
questions.why: Reggae guitar and keys play on the offbeat.

questions.q: A tie between two quarter notes of the same pitch creates what length?
questions.why: A tie joins durations: 1 + 1 = 2 beats.

questions.q: What is a polyrhythm?
o: One plain steady beat on its own
A loud final chord at the end
questions.why: Poly means many.

questions.q: A bar of 4/4 has these durations: 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 0.5. How many beats in total?
Match the term to its idea.
questions.why: Each is a rhythm tool.

questions.q: Why does syncopation make music feel energetic?
questions.model: The steady beat sets up an expectation and the accents land away from it, creating surprise and a pushing, dancing feeling.
questions.why: Playing against a steady beat creates energy.

questions.q: A drum stresses beats 2 and 4 in 4/4. Is it syncopated?
o: Yes, any stress on 2 and 4 is syncopation
Not necessarily, it uses the weaker beats but still lands on the beat
It has no real beat to speak of
Only if the piece is written in 3/4
questions.why: Backbeat stresses beats 2 and 4. True syncopation emphasises offbeat positions or ties across the beat.

panel.q: Why do dancers still feel the beat in syncopated music?
o: The steady pulse continues underneath the accents
The beat really does stop for them
The tempo secretly doubles in speed
panel.why: The pulse never goes away.

panel.q: How could a tie be used to write syncopation across a bar line?
panel.model: A note on the last beat of one bar is tied to the next bar, so the sound begins off the strong beat and carries over the downbeat.
panel.why: Ties show held notes crossing the beat.

panel.q: West African music often layers rhythms. What is this called?
panel.why: Cross-rhythms in many African traditions are polyrhythms.

teach.model: Syncopation puts the stress on weak or off-beat places instead of the strong beats. The steady beat carries on, and the accents push against it. Reggae and Afro-Cuban music use it a lot.

stages.title: Ear training
stages.hook: Can you recognise two notes as a perfect fifth the way you recognise a friend's voice? What helps?
explain: Ear training is learning to hear musical ideas and name them. You can learn to recognise intervals, chord qualities, scale types and rhythms. Like any skill it grows with short, regular practice.

Intervals have their own character. A perfect fifth (7 semitones) sounds open and strong; the first jump in the nursery tune "Twinkle, Twinkle" (C up to G) is a perfect fifth. A major third (4 semitones) sounds bright and a minor third (3) darker. An octave (12) sounds like the same note at two heights. A tritone (6) sounds tense.

Chords: a major triad sounds bright, a minor triad darker. Rhythm: tap what you hear back, then write it. Hearing the tonic helps you place every other note in a key, which is why singing the scale is part of ear training. Reference songs help, but the best method is to sing the interval too.

example.q: You hear C then E♭ (60 then 63). What interval is it?
steps: Count semitones: 63 − 60 = 3.
Three semitones is a minor third.
It sounds slightly dark compared with C to E.

analogies.home: You know people by voice. With practice you know intervals by sound.
analogies.city: You can tell a bus from a bicycle by sound before you see it.
analogies.nature: Bird-watchers name birds by their calls.
analogies.music: Singing back each note helps lock it into memory.

stages.mnemonic: Hear it, sing it, name it.
terms: Learning to recognise musical sounds by listening.
Writing down music that you hear.

misc.wrong: Ear training is only for people born with perfect pitch.
misc.right: Relative pitch can be learned by anyone with regular practice.

trip.prompt: Find the exercises on the page. Which one would you try first?

questions.q: Listen. What interval is this?
questions.why: 60 to 67 is seven semitones.

questions.q: Listen to the next pair. What interval is it?
questions.why: 60 to 64 is four semitones.

questions.q: Now this pair. What interval is it?
questions.why: 60 to 63 is three semitones.

questions.q: And this pair. What interval is it?
questions.why: 60 to 72 is twelve semitones.

questions.q: One more pair. What interval is it?
questions.why: 60 to 65 is five semitones.

questions.q: Listen. Is this chord major or minor?
questions.why: The notes 57, 60, 64 form A minor.

questions.q: Listen to this second chord. Is it major or minor?
questions.why: The notes 55, 59, 62 form G major.

questions.q: Match the interval to its size in semitones.
questions.why: These are standard sizes.

questions.q: You hear the two notes 64 and 71. How many semitones apart are they?
questions.why: 71 − 64 = 7, a perfect fifth.

questions.q: Suggest two ways to improve at ear training.
questions.model: Practise a little each day and sing what you hear. Use reference tunes, write down melodies and tap back rhythms.
questions.why: Regular active listening builds relative pitch.

panel.q: Why do many teachers ask you to sing the interval?
o: It makes you sound louder to others
It can take the place of listening
It changes the interval you hear
Singing connects your hearing and your voice
panel.why: Producing the sound reinforces recognition.

panel.q: Why is relative pitch more useful than perfect pitch for most musicians?
panel.model: Relative pitch lets you recognise the relationships between notes in any key, so you can follow, transpose and play with others even in unfamiliar tunings.
panel.why: Relationships matter in music.

panel.q: Two notes 6 semitones apart sound tense. Which interval is this?
panel.why: Six semitones is a tritone.

teach.model: Ear training means learning to recognise music by listening. Each interval has its own sound, like a perfect fifth that sounds open and a minor third that sounds darker. Major and minor chords also sound different. Regular practice and singing help.

points.ask: What do you do in ear training?

stages.title: Music reading
stages.hook: A page of music looks like a puzzle. What clues tell you what to play before you play a single note?
explain: Reading music means decoding the notation. Before you play, scan the clef, the key signature, the time signature, the tempo marking and the dynamics. This tells you the note names, which notes are sharp or flat, how to count, how fast and how loud.

A key signature is a set of sharps or flats at the start of each staff. No sharps or flats means C major (or A minor). One sharp (F♯) means G major, two sharps (F♯, C♯) means D major, and one flat (B♭) means F major. The sharps appear in the order F C G D A E B.

Sight-reading is playing or singing a new piece with little preparation. Good readers look ahead, keep a steady pulse and do not stop for mistakes. Reading rhythm first, by clapping it, makes the notes easier. Other systems exist too, such as tablature, solfège and Chinese jianpu numbers.

example.q: A piece has one sharp (F♯) in the key signature. Which major key is it?
steps: One sharp in the order F C G D A E B is F♯.
Key with one sharp is G major.
So every F in the piece is played as F♯.

analogies.home: Reading a recipe: check ingredients and steps before cooking.
analogies.city: A map has a key; check it first.
analogies.sport: Check the game plan before kickoff.
analogies.tech: A programmer reads a file header before running code.

stages.mnemonic: Clef, key, time, tempo: scan before you play.
terms: Sharps or flats at the start of the staff that apply throughout the piece.
Notation showing where to place fingers on a string instrument.
Naming notes with syllables such as do re mi.

misc.wrong: Reading music means you must play perfectly.
misc.right: Reading is a skill. Steady pulse and continuing after errors are more important than stopping to fix each note.

trip.prompt: Find the circle of fifths picture. Which key has two sharps?

questions.q: What does a key signature show?
o: How loudly each note is played
Which notes are sharp or flat
Where a player should take a breath
How many beats are in every bar
questions.why: It sets the sharps and flats for the piece.

questions.q: Which major key has no sharps or flats?
questions.why: C major uses only white keys.

questions.q: Which major key has one sharp?
questions.why: G major has F♯.

questions.q: Which major key has one flat?
questions.why: F major has B♭.

o: Only the title at the top of the page
Clef, key, time signature and tempo
Only the very last bar of the piece
Only the dynamics marked in the music
questions.why: These guide the whole piece.

questions.q: Match each term to what it is.
pairs: Sharps or flats at the start
questions.why: Different reading tools.

questions.q: Put the sharps in the order they appear in key signatures.
questions.why: The order is F C G D A E B.

questions.q: A piece in D major has two sharps. Which?
questions.why: D major has F♯ and C♯.

questions.q: Why should a sight-reader clap the rhythm first?
questions.model: Separating rhythm from pitch lets you get the counting right first, so the notes are easier to add.
questions.why: Reading one thing at a time lowers the load.

questions.q: When sight-reading, you play a wrong note. What is best?
o: Stop and restart after each slip
Give up on the piece altogether

Keep the pulse going and continue
questions.why: Keeping the beat is a core sight-reading rule.

panel.q: Why does the key signature use sharps and flats at the start, not before every note?
o: To make readers a little confused
To make the music sound louder
To avoid repeating them and to show the key
Because notes are not allowed accidentals
panel.why: Key signatures apply throughout the piece.

panel.q: Why do some musicians prefer tablature or jianpu to staff notation?
panel.model: They can be simpler to learn and fit the instrument or tradition, such as showing frets on guitar or numbered scale degrees.
panel.why: Notation systems suit different needs.

panel.q: Why is scanning ahead helpful when sight-reading?
o: It makes you stop between notes
You can prepare for what is coming
It hides all the mistakes you make
panel.why: Looking ahead keeps the music flowing.

teach.model: To read a piece, first scan the clef, key signature, time signature and tempo. The key signature tells you which notes are sharp or flat. In sight-reading, keep a steady pulse and carry on after a mistake. Reading the rhythm first can help.

points.ask: What do I look at first?
What does the key signature do?
What do I do if I make a mistake?
Is there a trick to make it easier?

stages.title: Singing and vocal technique
stages.hook: A good singer can fill a hall without a microphone and still sing for years. What is their secret?
explain: Singing starts with breath. Support the voice with low, relaxed breathing: the belly and lower ribs expand as the diaphragm moves down. The breath then flows steadily past the vocal folds in the larynx, which vibrate to make the sound. The mouth, throat and head shape that sound and act as resonators.

Posture matters: a tall, relaxed spine and loose jaw and shoulders. Warm up gently with humming, lip trills and light scales before louder singing. The voice has registers, such as chest voice and head voice, and singers learn to move smoothly between them.

Choirs usually sort voices into soprano, alto, tenor and bass (SATB), from highest to lowest. Voice care: drink water, avoid shouting or pushing, and rest when hoarse. Every culture has vocal traditions, from Mongolian throat singing to yodelling and Indian classical vocals.

example.q: A choir has four parts. List them from highest to lowest.
steps: The usual four are SATB.
Soprano is highest, then alto.
Then tenor, and bass is lowest.

analogies.home: Blowing up a balloon: steady breath makes steady sound.
analogies.sport: Athletes warm up before the race. Singers warm up the voice.
analogies.city: A trumpet needs air; a voice needs breath support too.
analogies.nature: A flute of air through a hollow stem: the body shapes the sound.

stages.mnemonic: Breath low, back tall, jaw loose, start small.
terms: The big muscle under the lungs that helps us breathe in.
Two small folds in the larynx that vibrate to make voice.
A range of the voice, such as chest or head voice.
Soprano, alto, tenor and bass choir parts.

misc.wrong: Singing louder means pushing from the throat.
misc.right: Loud singing comes from breath support and resonance. Pushing the throat strains the voice.

stages.limits: Voice teachers describe technique in different ways and traditions vary, but healthy singing is relaxed, supported and not strained.

trip.prompt: Find a diagram of the vocal folds and larynx.

questions.q: What part of the body vibrates to make voice?
questions.why: The vocal folds in the larynx vibrate as air passes.

questions.q: Which choir part is the highest?
questions.why: Soprano is the highest of SATB.

questions.q: Which choir part is the lowest?
questions.why: Bass is the lowest of SATB.

questions.q: What should you do before loud singing?
questions.why: Warm-ups prepare the voice.

o: Tension blocks the free flow of sound
It makes you look a little taller
It changes the key of the song

questions.why: Relaxation helps the sound resonate.

questions.q: Match the voice part to a description.
questions.why: Choir voices are named by range.

questions.q: A singer feels hoarse. What is the best response?

questions.q: Why is breath support important in singing?
questions.model: Steady air flow lets the vocal folds vibrate evenly and supports long phrases, so the tone is controlled and not strained.
questions.why: Air powers the voice.

questions.q: Which tradition is known for singing two pitches at once?

panel.q: Why do singers hum or trill their lips to warm up?
o: It makes the voice louder, and that is all

panel.why: High notes come from technique, not force.

teach.model: Good singing starts with low, relaxed breathing and a tall posture. The air makes the vocal folds vibrate and the mouth and head shape the sound. Warm up gently, drink water and rest when your voice is tired.

points.ask: How do I look after my voice?

stages.title: Piano and keyboard skills
stages.hook: The piano has 88 keys and ten fingers to play them. How do pianists find their way without looking?
explain: The piano keyboard has a repeating pattern of black keys in groups of two and three. The white key just left of a group of two black keys is C. Learning these landmarks lets you find any note quickly. Middle C is near the centre of the keyboard.

Fingers are numbered 1 to 5 starting with the thumb as 1, in each hand. Sit tall with relaxed wrists, curved fingers and your forearms level. In a C position the right hand thumb plays C and the fingers play D E F G. The left hand mirrors it, with the little finger (5) on the lowest note.

To play the C major scale, the thumb passes under the hand after finger 3 (right hand) so the fingering stays smooth. Keyboards include pedals: the sustain pedal on a piano lifts the dampers so notes ring on. Electronic keyboards share the layout and can change sounds.

example.q: How do you find middle C on a keyboard?
steps: Look for a group of two black keys near the centre.
The white key just to the left of the two black keys is C.
Choose the C closest to the middle: middle C.
example.a: The white key left of the two black keys near the centre

analogies.home: Doors in a corridor with patterns of two and three to know where you are.
analogies.city: Landmarks in a city help you find your way.
analogies.nature: Constellations show where you are in the sky.
analogies.tech: A keyboard layout is a map of notes.

stages.mnemonic: C is left of the two; thumb is one.
terms: Numbering of fingers (1 = thumb) to guide which finger plays which note.
The piano pedal that lets notes keep ringing.
A pattern on the keyboard, such as two black keys together, that helps you find a note.
The C near the centre of the keyboard (MIDI 60).

misc.wrong: You should look at your hands all the time.
misc.right: Learn the landmarks and keep your eyes on the music; your hands learn the distances by feel.

questions.q: Why do pianists learn keyboard landmarks like the groups of black keys?
questions.model: The pattern lets them find any note quickly without looking down, so they can read music and keep playing.
questions.why: Landmarks allow touch navigation.

panel.q: Why does the thumb pass under in a scale?
o: So that the notes are hidden
So the hand can keep going smoothly past five notes
So that the scale sounds louder
panel.why: A hand covers five notes, so the thumb moves to the next position.

panel.q: What are some safe habits to avoid sore hands when practising?
panel.model: Sit tall, keep wrists and shoulders relaxed, warm up, take short breaks and stop if there is pain.
panel.why: Tension and long sessions cause strain.

panel.q: An electronic keyboard has 61 keys. What is different from a piano?
o: It has fewer keys and can change sounds
It has no black keys at all
It is not really a keyboard
It has no octaves in it
panel.why: The layout is the same but the range is smaller.

teach.model: The piano keys follow a pattern of black keys in twos and threes. C is the white key just left of the two black keys. Fingers are numbered with the thumb as 1. Sit tall with relaxed wrists and curved fingers.

stages.title: Guitar and percussion skills
stages.hook: Guitar and drums look totally different, but both rely on a steady pulse. How do their players keep it?
explain: A standard guitar has six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, E A D G B E. Pressing a string against a fret shortens the vibrating length and raises the pitch by one semitone per fret. The 12th fret gives the octave of the open string. Chords are shapes held with the left hand while the right hand strums or picks.
Guitar skills: keep a steady strum, change chords smoothly, and use a capo to raise the pitch of every string. Bass guitar has four lower strings (E A D G, an octave below the guitar's lowest four).

Percussion includes drums and many hand instruments. A drum kit has a bass drum, snare, toms and cymbals; the hi-hat often keeps time. Around the world, hand drums such as the djembe (West Africa), conga (Cuba), tabla (India) and bodhran (Ireland) give strong rhythmic traditions. A good percussionist plays with a relaxed grip and listens for the pulse.

example.q: The open low E string is MIDI 40. Fretting it at the 5th fret gives which note?
steps: Each fret adds 1 semitone.
45 is the open A string, A2.

analogies.home: Pressing a rubber band shorter makes it sound higher.
analogies.farm: A small bell rings higher than a big cowbell.
analogies.sport: A drummer is like a team coach keeping everyone in time.
analogies.music: Strumming down and up keeps your hand moving in steady eighth notes.

terms: A raised bar on the neck of a guitar, one semitone apart.
A clamp that raises the pitch of all strings.
Brushing across several strings with a pick or fingers.
A pair of cymbals on a stand, often used to keep time.

misc.right: Steady time and good tone matter more than speed for both guitar and drums.

Shorter strings become tighter at once
Shorter strings stop vibrating at all

panel.q: Why might a drummer and a bass player practise together?
panel.model: They form the rhythm section and need to lock together so the whole band has a solid pulse.

teach.model: A guitar has six strings tuned E A D G B E. Each fret raises the pitch by one semitone. Drums and hand percussion keep the beat, and the hi-hat often keeps steady time. Good players keep the pulse steady and listen to others.

stages.title: Composition fundamentals
stages.hook: Where do songs come from? Could you write an eight-bar tune in ten minutes using only three ideas?
explain: Composition is creating new music. A simple method is: choose a mood, pick a key and time signature, invent a motif, build a melody from it, add a chord progression and decide the form. Even a few minutes of experiment can begin a piece.

Form is the plan of a piece. Common forms are AB (two contrasting sections), ABA (statement, contrast, return) and verse-chorus. Contrast keeps interest, and repetition gives unity. Too much repetition is dull; too much change loses the listener.

Composers record ideas by writing notation, using tablature or lead sheets, or by recording audio. Composition happens all over the world: some traditions compose in writing, others pass music orally and shape it through performance. Edit your work: listen back, then remove or change what does not help.

example.q: Plan an ABA piece. What happens in each section?
steps: A: state the main tune.
B: a contrasting section, perhaps in a different key or rhythm.
A: the main tune returns.
example.a: Main tune, contrast, return of main tune

analogies.city: Designing a park with a path that returns to the gate.
analogies.farm: Plant, grow, harvest: a form that comes round.
analogies.sport: A game plan with a surprise move.

terms: The overall plan or structure of a piece.
A form where the first section returns after a contrast.
A simple notation with melody and chord symbols.

misc.wrong: Composers wait for inspiration and then write the whole piece.
misc.right: Most composers work step by step: try ideas, repeat, change and edit.

It removes the key from the piece
It gives unity and helps memory

questions.why: Revision is part of composing.

questions.q: In many oral traditions, how is music passed on?
o: By listening and performing, not only by writing
Only by writing it down on paper

panel.q: Why is a motif a good starting point for composing?

It brings the whole piece to an end
It takes the place of harmony
It gives a small idea to develop
panel.why: Developing a motif creates unity.

panel.q: How could you make a B section contrast with an A section?
panel.model: Change something noticeable: the key, rhythm, tempo, register, dynamics or instrument so the B section feels fresh.
panel.why: Contrast changes at least one ingredient.

panel.q: A composer shares a melody orally with a group who then adapt it. What does this show?

Music must never be changed at all

Only a single person can ever compose
panel.why: Oral traditions allow collective change.

teach.model: To compose, choose a mood, key and time signature. Invent a motif, build a melody and add chords. Plan the form such as ABA so there is both repetition and contrast. Then listen back and edit.
